text.text: A learner that is willing to credit any event it experienced with causing an outcome has nothing to prefer among the many coincidences in its past, so it either needs a great deal of data or locks onto a spurious rule. A learner that comes equipped with a prior restriction on what may cause what (an inductive bias) can learn from very little data, but only as long as the world respects the restriction: the same restriction makes it unable to learn when the cause lies outside what it allows.The two classical illustrations are the rat that avoids a bait after a single bout of nausea, because it considers only what it ate as a possible cause of sickness, and Skinner's pigeons, fed at fixed intervals whatever they did, several of which developed a repeated ritual that they apparently believed brought the food.Holds when Illustrative simulation. The pigeon rule (credit to the behaviour in progress at feeding; choice proportional to credit squared) and the rat's hypothesis search are toy models chosen to show the effect, not fits to the animal data.

Learning from a sample is an inference from finitely many observed cases to the unseen ones, and a finite sample is consistent with many explanations. If every one of FFF cues may be the cause, then after nnn poisonings the cues that happened to be present every time are still all candidates: the true cause plus each other cue with probability 2−n2^{-n}2−n, so the number of impostors is binomial with F−1F-1F−1 trials and success probability p=2−np=2^{-n}p=2−n, and a learner choosing uniformly among the candidates is right with probability E[11+K]=1−(1−p)FFp\mathbb E\big[\tfrac1{1+K}\big]=\dfrac{1-(1-p)^F}{Fp}E[1+K1​]=Fp1−(1−p)F​ (about 1/(1+(F−1)p)1/(1+(F-1)p)1/(1+(F−1)p) when FFF is small). Restricting the candidates to the taste of the bait removes the competition at once. The price is exactly the price paid in the No-Free-Lunch theorem (ml-5.1): a restriction that does not match the world gives a learner that never succeeds. The pigeon is the other face of the coin: with no prior against "my wing flap brings food", credit given to whatever it was doing when food arrived feeds back into what it does next, and a ritual is born.For F≥1F\ge1F≥1 and p>0p>0p>0, write 1/(k+1)=∫01tk dt1/(k+1)=\int_0^1t^k\,dt1/(k+1)=∫01​tkdt. The binomial theorem (comb 1.7) turns the finite weighted sum for the success probability into ∫01(1−p+pt)F−1 dt\int_0^1(1-p+pt)^{F-1}\,dt∫01​(1−p+pt)F−1dt. The fundamental theorem (pma 6.21) evaluates this polynomial integral as [1−(1−p)F]/(Fp)[1-(1-p)^F]/(Fp)[1−(1−p)F]/(Fp). This derives the stated toy-model average rather than replacing the random number of competitors by its mean.The rat calculation assumes an idealized sampling model: the true cause is present at every poisoned meal, while each irrelevant cue is independently present with probability 1/21/21/2 at each meal, independently across cues as well. A particular irrelevant cue survives nnn meals exactly when the product of its nnn presence indicators is 111; the independent-product expectation rule (PROB 2.1.13) makes its survival probability 2−n2^{-n}2−n. Survival indicators for different cues are measurable functions of disjoint independent cue columns, so the independent-block argument (PROB 2.1.10) makes them independent. Their sum is therefore binomial, supplying the premise of the finite expectation calculation above. The code illustrates this ideal model with separate seeded draws per cue and meal; neither genuine independence of a deterministic generator nor a model fitted to animal cognition is claimed.

text.text: A learner that is willing to credit any event it experienced with causing an outcome has nothing to prefer among the many coincidences in its past, so it either needs a great deal of data or locks onto a spurious rule. A learner that comes equipped with a prior restriction on what may cause what (an inductive bias) can learn from very little data, but only as long as the world respects the restriction: the same restriction makes it unable to learn when the cause lies outside what it allows.The two classical illustrations are the rat that avoids a bait after a single bout of nausea, because it considers only what it ate as a possible cause of sickness, and Skinner's pigeons, fed at fixed intervals whatever they did, several of which developed a repeated ritual that they apparently believed brought the food.Holds when Illustrative simulation. The pigeon rule (credit to the behaviour in progress at feeding; choice proportional to credit squared) and the rat's hypothesis search are toy models chosen to show the effect, not fits to the animal data.

Learning from a sample is an inference from finitely many observed cases to the unseen ones, and a finite sample is consistent with many explanations. If every one of FFF cues may be the cause, then after nnn poisonings the cues that happened to be present every time are still all candidates: the true cause plus each other cue with probability 2−n2^{-n}2−n, so the number of impostors is binomial with F−1F-1F−1 trials and success probability p=2−np=2^{-n}p=2−n, and a learner choosing uniformly among the candidates is right with probability E[11+K]=1−(1−p)FFp\mathbb E\big[\tfrac1{1+K}\big]=\dfrac{1-(1-p)^F}{Fp}E[1+K1​]=Fp1−(1−p)F​ (about 1/(1+(F−1)p)1/(1+(F-1)p)1/(1+(F−1)p) when FFF is small). Restricting the candidates to the taste of the bait removes the competition at once. The price is exactly the price paid in the No-Free-Lunch theorem (ml-5.1): a restriction that does not match the world gives a learner that never succeeds. The pigeon is the other face of the coin: with no prior against "my wing flap brings food", credit given to whatever it was doing when food arrived feeds back into what it does next, and a ritual is born.For F≥1F\ge1F≥1 and p>0p>0p>0, write 1/(k+1)=∫01tk dt1/(k+1)=\int_0^1t^k\,dt1/(k+1)=∫01​tkdt. The binomial theorem (comb 1.7) turns the finite weighted sum for the success probability into ∫01(1−p+pt)F−1 dt\int_0^1(1-p+pt)^{F-1}\,dt∫01​(1−p+pt)F−1dt. The fundamental theorem (pma 6.21) evaluates this polynomial integral as [1−(1−p)F]/(Fp)[1-(1-p)^F]/(Fp)[1−(1−p)F]/(Fp). This derives the stated toy-model average rather than replacing the random number of competitors by its mean.The rat calculation assumes an idealized sampling model: the true cause is present at every poisoned meal, while each irrelevant cue is independently present with probability 1/21/21/2 at each meal, independently across cues as well. A particular irrelevant cue survives nnn meals exactly when the product of its nnn presence indicators is 111; the independent-product expectation rule (PROB 2.1.13) makes its survival probability 2−n2^{-n}2−n. Survival indicators for different cues are measurable functions of disjoint independent cue columns, so the independent-block argument (PROB 2.1.10) makes them independent. Their sum is therefore binomial, supplying the premise of the finite expectation calculation above. The code illustrates this ideal model with separate seeded draws per cue and meal; neither genuine independence of a deterministic generator nor a model fitted to animal cognition is claimed.

statement-scope.text: A learner that is willing to credit any event it experienced with causing an outcome has nothing to prefer among the many coincidences in its past, so it either needs a great deal of data or locks onto a spurious rule. A learner that comes equipped with a prior restriction on what may cause what (an inductive bias) can learn from very little data, but only as long as the world respects the restriction: the same restriction makes it unable to learn when the cause lies outside what it allows.The two classical illustrations are the rat that avoids a bait after a single bout of nausea, because it considers only what it ate as a possible cause of sickness, and Skinner's pigeons, fed at fixed intervals whatever they did, several of which developed a repeated ritual that they apparently believed brought the food.Illustrative simulation. The pigeon rule (credit to the behaviour in progress at feeding; choice proportional to credit squared) and the rat's hypothesis search are toy models chosen to show the effect, not fits to the animal data.

statement-scope.text: A learner that is willing to credit any event it experienced with causing an outcome has nothing to prefer among the many coincidences in its past, so it either needs a great deal of data or locks onto a spurious rule. The pigeon rule (credit to the behaviour in progress at feeding; choice proportional to credit squared) and the rat's hypothesis search are toy models chosen to show the effect, not fits to the animal data.
